In 1999, British solicitor Sally Clark was convicted of murdering her two infant sons. The prosecution’s key evidence? Pediatrician Sir Roy Meadow testified that the probability of two children in the same family dying of sudden infant death syndrome (SIDS) was 1 in 73 million — so it
The jury convicted. Sally Clark went to prison.
But the statistic was catastrophically wrong. Meadow had confused two very different questions:
“What is the probability that two children die of SIDS?”
“What is the probability that a mother is innocent, given that two children died?”

children.value: — and the difference between them is not a technicality. It is the difference between freedom and prison.
Meadow arrived at 1 in 73 million by squaring the single-SIDS rate of 1 in 8,543 — implicitly assuming the two deaths were

. But SIDS deaths within a family share genetic and environmental risk factors. The actual conditional probability of a second SIDS death given the first was closer to 1 in 60–130, not 1 in 8,543. The Royal Statistical Society issued a formal public rebuke of the misuse of statistics in Clark’s trial.
After a lengthy appeal, Clark was exonerated in January 2003 and released after more than three years in prison. She never recovered and died in 2007.

Understanding conditional probability is not just mathematics. It is a matter of justice, of life and death, and of getting the right answer when the stakes are highest. By the end of this chapter, you will understand exactly
the prosecution’s argument was wrong — and you will have the mathematical tools to never make the same mistake.
